interviewQuestions.question: How would you design a data structure that supports adding numbers from a stream and finding the current median in O(log n) insert and O(1) query?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I split the data across two heaps: a max-heap holding the lower half of values seen so far, and a min-heap holding the upper half. Each heap type is chosen deliberately so its root is exactly the boundary value closest to the median — the max-heap's root is the largest of the small values, the min-heap's root is the smallest of the large values.

I maintain two invariants on every insert: the two heaps' sizes never differ by more than one, and every value in the max-heap is ≤ every value in the min-heap. To insert correctly, I push the new value into the max-heap first, then immediately move that heap's new maximum into the min-heap, then move it back if that made the min-heap too big. That transfer-then-rebalance sequence is what guarantees both invariants simultaneously — pushing in based on a naive comparison against the current median alone can silently violate one or both invariants without erroring.

Reading the median is then O(1): if the max-heap has one extra element, its root is the median directly; if the sizes are equal, the median is the average of both roots.

Insert costs O(log n) for the heap operations; median lookup costs O(1) — a real improvement over re-sorting on every insert, which would be O(n log n) per element.

**Testing:** whether you understand why the transfer-based insert is necessary, not just that two heaps are involved.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between the size-balance invariant and the ordering invariant in the two-heap median finder, and why do you need both?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The size-balance invariant says the two heaps' sizes differ by at most one — this alone guarantees I know *which* heap (or the average of both) holds the median by count. The ordering invariant says every value in the max-heap is ≤ every value in the min-heap — this guarantees the split is actually positioned at the true median, not just at some arbitrary size-balanced cut point.

They're independent properties, and maintaining only one isn't enough. Imagine size balance holds perfectly, but the ordering invariant has been violated — say a value that should be in the upper half got pushed into the max-heap instead. The heaps are still equal-sized, `find_median()` will still run without error, and it will return a specific number — just the wrong one, since the max-heap's root no longer represents the actual lower-half boundary.

That's why a correct insert can't just check sizes and push into whichever heap 'looks smaller' — it has to actively route the new value through both heaps (push into one, transfer the resulting extreme into the other) so that both invariants are re-established together on every single insert, not just approximately maintained over time.

I'd frame this as a common shortcut mistake: implementing only the size-balancing half of the logic looks correct on many test cases and only fails on inputs where a value needs to cross the boundary in a way the shortcut doesn't handle.

**Testing:** whether you understand both invariants are load-bearing and independently necessary, not redundant with each other.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Invariants

interviewQuestions.question: How would you extend this to a running median over a sliding window of the last k elements, and what makes that harder than the unbounded-stream version?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The unbounded-stream version never needs to remove anything — every value stays forever. A sliding window adds a requirement the basic two-heap trick doesn't handle at all: I need to **evict** the element that just aged out of the window, and that element is essentially arbitrary from the heap's perspective — it's very unlikely to be sitting at either heap's root.

A standard heap only supports efficient removal of its root; finding and removing an arbitrary interior element would require a linear scan, which defeats the point of using a heap in the first place.

The practical workaround mirrors the decrease-key gap from the priority-queues topic: **lazy deletion**. I track, in a separate hash map, how many times each value is currently 'pending removal.' When a value ages out of the window, I don't touch the heap directly — I just increment its pending-removal count. Whenever a root happens to be a value with a nonzero pending-removal count (checked during a rebalance step or a median read), I pop it, decrement its count, and treat the heap as if that element was never there, continuing to the next root if needed.

The subtlety this adds: the two heaps' *raw* sizes (including not-yet-cleaned-up stale entries) can drift out of the strict ±1 balance, so the balance invariant has to be checked against each heap's *logical* size (raw size minus pending removals for elements known to be in that heap), not its raw size — a real extra layer of bookkeeping beyond the basic version.

**Testing:** whether you can identify exactly what capability is missing (arbitrary removal) and apply the standard fix (lazy deletion) rather than assuming the same two-heap code just works unchanged.
